title: Classification and cladistics
summary: Why biologists classify organisms, how cladograms built from DNA and protein sequences reveal evolutionary relationships, and how this has reshaped classification into three domains.

keyterms.definition: Arranging organisms into groups; needed to organise the huge diversity of life and help scientists communicate and make predictions.
A group of organisms at any level of classification, e.g. a species, genus or family.
The traditional ranks: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species, with each taxon nested in the next.
Classification in which each group contains all descendants of a common ancestor, so it reflects evolutionary relationships and allows predictions.
A group of organisms consisting of a common ancestor and all of its descendants, sharing characteristics inherited from that ancestor.
A branching diagram showing the most probable sequence of divergence of clades.
A branch point on a cladogram, representing a hypothetical common ancestor where two clades diverged.
The base of a cladogram, representing the common ancestor of all the organisms shown.
Using the number of sequence differences between species to estimate the time since they diverged from a common ancestor.
The principle of choosing the cladogram that requires the fewest evolutionary changes (e.g. sequence changes) to explain the data.
The highest taxonomic rank; all organisms are classified into Archaea, Bacteria or Eukarya.
Comparison of rRNA base sequences by Woese and colleagues, which revealed that prokaryotes form two very distinct groups, Archaea and Bacteria.
Cladistic analysis showed the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae) was not a clade, so many genera were moved to other families.

questions.prompt: Order the traditional taxonomic ranks from broadest to narrowest.
questions.explanation: Each kingdom contains phyla, each phylum classes, and so on down to genus and then species.

questions.prompt: Why is it difficult to classify organisms into the traditional hierarchy of taxa?
options: Because there are too few species
Because organisms do not vary
Because species evolve and branch continuously, so ranks like 'order' or 'family' have no fixed meaning in nature
Because DNA cannot be compared between species
questions.explanation: Evolution produces a continuous branching tree, not distinct levels. Deciding whether a group is a family or an order is arbitrary, and different groups do not match rank for rank.

questions.statement: A clade includes a common ancestor and all of its descendants.
questions.explanation: A clade must include every descendant of the ancestor. Leaving any out (e.g. 'reptiles' without birds) does not form a clade.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a classification that corresponds to evolutionary relationships?
options: It is easier to memorise
It allows predictions: a feature found in one member is likely to occur in others of the group
It groups organisms by habitat
It needs no evidence from DNA
questions.explanation: Members of a natural group share ancestry, so characteristics (e.g. a useful chemical in a plant) are likely to be found in related species too.

questions.text: A group consisting of a common ancestor and all its descendants is a ___.
questions.explanation: Clades are defined by common ancestry. A taxon is any named group, which may or may not be a clade.

questions.prompt: Match each domain to a feature or example.

pairs.right: Prokaryotes such as Bacillus and cyanobacteria
Prokaryotes often from extreme habitats, e.g. methanogens
Organisms with nucleus: animals, plants, fungi, protists

questions.explanation: rRNA evidence showed that prokaryotes form two domains as different from each other as from eukaryotes.

questions.prompt: What evidence led to the classification of all organisms into three domains?
options: Base sequences of ribosomal RNA
Shape of cells under a light microscope
Presence or absence of a cell wall
Mode of nutrition
questions.explanation: Carl Woese compared rRNA sequences and found prokaryotes split into two deeply divergent groups, Bacteria and Archaea, alongside Eukarya.

questions.statement: Archaea are more closely related to Bacteria than to Eukarya because both are prokaryotes.
questions.explanation: Despite both being prokaryotic, rRNA and other molecular evidence show Archaea share a more recent common ancestor with Eukarya than with Bacteria.

questions.text: The highest rank of classification, above kingdom, is the ___.
questions.explanation: There are three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

questions.prompt: Why do biologists need to classify organisms?
options: To reduce the number of species on Earth
To prove that species never change
To give each species a common name
To organise the vast diversity of life so it can be studied, identified and discussed
questions.explanation: With millions of species, an agreed classification system lets biologists find information, identify organisms and communicate internationally.

questions.prompt: What does a node on a cladogram represent?
options: A living species
A hypothetical common ancestor where lineages diverged
An extinction event
The age of a fossil
questions.explanation: Each node is a branching point representing the common ancestor of all the clades branching from it. Living species are at the terminal branch tips.

questions.statement: The more differences there are between the base sequences of a gene in two species, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.
questions.explanation: The opposite: differences accumulate gradually over time, so more differences indicate a longer time since divergence.

questions.text: Choosing the cladogram that requires the fewest evolutionary changes uses the principle of ___.
questions.explanation: Parsimony assumes the simplest explanation, with the fewest sequence changes, is the most probable.

questions.prompt: Why are base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins useful for constructing cladograms?
options: Sequence differences accumulate gradually, so the number of differences reflects how closely species are related
Sequences never change, so all species share them
Morphology is always more reliable than sequences
Only proteins can be compared between species
questions.explanation: Sequence data are objective and numerous, and they avoid being misled by convergent evolution of similar-looking structures.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a cladogram to what it represents.

pairs.right: Common ancestor of all organisms shown
A species or group at the tip

questions.explanation: A cladogram is read from the root outwards: nodes are splits and any node with everything beyond it forms a clade.

questions.prompt: Species A and B differ by 4 bases in a gene; A and C differ by 18; B and C differ by 17. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A and C are the most closely related
B and C share the most recent common ancestor
All three species diverged at the same time
A and B share a more recent common ancestor than either does with C
questions.explanation: The fewest differences (4) are between A and B, so they diverged most recently; C branched off earlier.

questions.statement: Cladograms are hypotheses that may be revised when new evidence is found.
questions.explanation: Cladograms show the most probable sequence of divergence based on current data; additional sequences can lead to different branching patterns.

questions.prompt: What did cladistic analysis reveal about the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae)?
options: It was a clade, confirming the traditional classification
It contained only one genus
It was not a true clade, so many genera were reclassified into other families
It belonged to the domain Archaea
questions.explanation: DNA-based cladistics showed the traditional figwort family grouped unrelated plants by similar morphology, so the family was split and many genera were moved.

questions.text: Estimating when clades diverged from the number of sequence differences uses the molecular ___.
questions.explanation: Assuming differences accumulate at a roughly constant rate, they can be converted to a time since divergence, calibrated with fossils.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for constructing a cladogram from sequence data.
items: Choose a gene or protein found in all the species
Count the differences between each pair of species
Group the most similar species together first
Draw the branching pattern requiring the fewest changes
questions.explanation: Aligned sequences are compared, species with fewest differences are joined at the most recent nodes, and parsimony selects the best tree.
